Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
ruminate about how event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma defined as witnessing domestic violence, 'Body Shame' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type because it implies a direct bodily violation or injury to the patient rather than witnessing violence between others. While witness trauma can lead to guilt, fear, mistrust, or betrayal appraisals, shame specifically about 'what happened to my body' is clinically implausible here unless there is an additional unreported direct trauma.

issues.item: Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
issues.explanation: The memory profile centers on disorganized, overwhelmed recall of a witnessed domestic violence event. 'Auditory Recall' can occur in witness trauma, but in this profile it is the only strongly sensory-perceptual memory item and is not linked to any trigger items or matching contextual content. Given the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from Memory and the rest of the profile emphasizes global threat and appraisal-driven coping, this item stands out as poorly integrated and may reflect a different trauma presentation.

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 26-year-old Salvadoran American woman who works as a school counselor at a middle school in the same city where she grew up. She presented for treatment describing a pattern of distress that she had, until recently, managed to attribute to stress or personality - something she had simply always been. It was only after a student disclosed a situation of domestic violence at home that Valentina found herself unable to function for the remainder of that school day, sitting in her car in the parking lot for over an hour, and she began to accept that what she was carrying was something older and heavier than work fatigue.

Valentina grew up in a two-bedroom apartment in a dense urban neighborhood, the eldest of three children. From approximately age seven through twelve, she witnessed her father's repeated violence toward her mother - eruptions that were sudden, physical, and loud, often occurring in the kitchen or living room with no warning that Valentina could reliably detect in advance. She described one incident with particular clarity: she had been sitting at the kitchen table doing homework when her father entered, and within seconds the room transformed. She remembered the sound of her mother's back hitting the refrigerator, the way the metal surface rang out, and her own paralysis - she had not moved, had not called for help, had not done anything. Her mother eventually left the relationship when Valentina was twelve, but by then the family had cycled through a brief period of contact with child protective services that resulted in no sustained intervention. Valentina had told a teacher once, obliquely. Nothing changed.

In the years that followed, Valentina constructed a life oriented around competence and care for others. She studied hard, earned a graduate degree, and chose a profession in which she could be the adult who actually listened to children. But the architecture of her daily life had quietly organized itself around the residue of those years. She had never returned to the neighborhood where she grew up, routing her commute to avoid even passing the street where the apartment building stood. The avoidance had become so automatic that she no longer consciously registered it as a choice.

At work, Valentina is warm and skilled with students, but colleagues have noticed that she tends to position herself near the wall in staff meetings, angling her chair so that the door remains in her sightline. She has come to feel that sitting with her back exposed is genuinely dangerous, not metaphorically uncomfortable but concretely unsafe, and she arranges herself accordingly in every room she enters, including her own apartment. Even there, she described a persistent sense of being on guard - checking the lock twice before bed, lying awake listening to the building settle. When a colleague placed a hand briefly on her shoulder during a difficult conversation about a student, Valentina's body responded before her mind could intervene: she startled sharply, knocking her coffee cup from the table, and spent the rest of the afternoon ashamed and over-explaining.

She scans people carefully, reading for signs of volatility - a raised voice in the hallway, a man who moves with a certain energy. She had come to believe, as a settled and rarely examined conviction, that people cannot be trusted to remain safe, that their surfaces are unreliable. This vigilance extended inward as well. She returned repeatedly, in quiet moments, to the night she sat frozen at the kitchen table, and she was certain that if she had acted differently - screamed, run, called someone - the years of violence might have unfolded otherwise. The logic was circular and she knew it intellectually, but the feeling of culpability did not yield to logic. She also carried a corrosive sense that the systems meant to protect her and her mother had simply looked away, and she understood her own career partly as a correction of that failure - though the knowledge that she now sat inside one of those same institutions complicated things.

When Valentina tries to explain what happened to her as a child, she loses the thread partway through, the narrative fragmenting into sensation and silence. The memory does not arrive in sequence; it arrives whole and without invitation, triggered by the ring of metal, by a raised voice in a classroom corridor, by the smell of a particular cleaning product. What finally brought her to seek help was not just the parking lot afternoon, but her recognition that she was becoming less present with her students - the very thing she had built her life to prevent. What she feared most, sitting across from the intake clinician, was that telling it would make it more real. What she hoped for, though she could barely say it aloud, was that it might finally become the past.
